slides.headline: When a forced restore is the wrong fix
slides.body: Had someone already built on the bad tip, the right move in Incident 2 would be git revert of the bad commits, which adds commits that undo them.

slides.headline: When a forced restore is the wrong fix
slides.body: One: keep the rewritten history and re-add the fix, with no further force, but then the deployed tag is never an ancestor again and every recorded ID points off-branch.

slides.headline: GitHub, not Git: the rule and the instruments
slides.body: A ruleset is GitHub's named list of rules for chosen branches.

slides.headline: GitHub, not Git: the rule and the instruments
slides.body: When no clone has the old value, GitHub offers instruments of its own.

lines.s: gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/git/refs -f ref=refs/heads/recovered -f sha=<commit ID from before the force

slides.headline: GitHub, not Git: the rule and the instruments
slides.body: GitHub documents each instrument and not this combined procedure, publishes no retention period for commits that no ref reaches, and documents no "restore" action inside the Activity view.
Think of the server's branch as a signpost at a junction, and of every clone as a traveller who photographed the signpost the last time they passed.
So the investigation is a collection of photographs.
Where the picture breaks: on GitHub there's a camera after all, the Activity view and the events, with limits and lifetimes of its own, and with the caveats you heard.
The model for the restoring push: say out loud what you believe the server holds, and let the server refuse if you're wrong.

slides.headline: From root cause to controls on several layers
slides.body: A client default: push.default left at simple.
Five mistakes to watch for.

items: Trusting git status about the server. Root cause: it compares with the remote-tracking branch, which is the clone's memory of the last contact.
Restoring with a bare --force. Root cause: nothing then checks whether somebody pushed to the branch in the meantime, so the recovery can remove a colleague's work.
Restoring without looking at what was built on the new tip. Root cause: a legitimate commit made after the rewrite sits on the history that is about to be replaced.

Advising "reset to the server" to someone who sees "diverged". Root cause: with no local commits, divergence means the server's history was replaced, and the reset makes a second clone adopt the rewrite.
Accepting "same code, fewer commits" without a tree comparison. Root cause: an interactive rebase can drop a commit with one deleted line of the todo list, and only the trees show it.

slides.body: Now, out of the lab. A billing team deploys from a branch named production.
The engineer on call writes one sentence in the channel, asks two colleagues not to fetch or reset, and collects three witnesses of the old tip …
She finds one legitimate commit on top of the rewrite, anchors the rewritten state, carries that commit over, and restores with a lease that names the server's current value.
Her summary rates the incident SEV 2 although nothing was deployed, because the only thing between the rewritten branch and production was that one check.
Your turn. Do Lab 37.1, "A force push to the wrong branch (incident 2)", in lab-manual/m37-incident-drills-platform.md, from a freshly generated sandbox.
Before you fetch, write down what you'll record first and why.
The challenge is Lab 37.2, "Production branch history is rewritten (incident 4)", in the same file.

slides.body: Read sections 30.6 and 30.8.
You can now put a replaced branch back without losing what a colleague built since, and say which control was missing on which layer.

beats.text: In both cases a shared branch on the server now points at a history that isn't the one everybody had. A branch is a named line of commits, the saved snapshots of a project. A force push overwrites the server's branch, so commits can drop off it. And "not an ancestor" means that the branch's history no longer contains the deployed commit. In both cases the obvious repair is another forced push, to put the old history back.

beats.text: Witnesses. When a server branch has been replaced, the old value is known to three kinds of witness. A clone that hasn't fetched since: its remote-tracking branch, the clone's record of the server's branch, still holds the old value. A clone that has fetched: the reflog of its remote-tracking branch holds the previous value as the entry before the forced update. And anything that recorded the commit by ID: a tag, which is a fixed name for one commit, or a deployment record.

beats.text: You can now put a replaced branch back without losing what a colleague built since, and say which control was missing on which layer. Practise the first restore by hand before you go on. Next time, a new report: "I pushed one commit and the pull request shows 500 files". Until then, look at the state first and type second. See you in the next one.
